cards.title: Hola is just the beginning
cards.body: Spanish greets by time of day: buenos días (good morning), buenas tardes (good afternoon), buenas noches (good evening/night). Hola works anytime, but matching the hour sounds instantly more natural.

cards.title: The four magic words
cards.body: Por favor (please), gracias (thank you), perdón (sorry/excuse me), and de nada (you're welcome) will carry you through almost any interaction. Learn these four before anything else and doors open.
The Spanish r: tap the tip of your tongue once against the ridge behind your teeth, like the 'tt' in 'butter' said fast. Pero (but) uses one tap; perro (dog) rolls it longer.

— ¡Hola! ¿Cómo estás? (Hi! How are you?)
— Muy bien, gracias. ¿Y tú? (Very well, thanks. And you?)
— ¡Buenos días! (Good morning!)

Three lines, one friendly exchange. Note the upside-down ¿ at the start of questions — it warns you a question is coming.

cards.q: Someone greets you at 9 AM. Most natural reply?
cards.explain: Buenos días covers the morning. Buenas noches is for night, and adiós means goodbye — the opposite of a greeting.

questions.q: It's 3 PM. You walk into a shop. You say…
questions.explain: Tardes covers afternoon until evening. Días is morning, noches is night.

questions.q: Someone holds the door for you. You say…
questions.explain: Gracias thanks them. Por favor asks for something; perdón apologizes.

questions.q: You bump into someone. You say…
questions.explain: Perdón excuses you. De nada answers a thank-you; hola just greets.

questions.q: A friend thanks you for help. You reply…
questions.explain: De nada means 'you're welcome' — literally 'of nothing.'

choices: Warns you a question is starting
questions.explain: Spanish puts ¿ at the start so you read the whole sentence with question intonation from the beginning.

cards.title: Two verbs for 'to be': ser vs estar
cards.body: Ser is for permanent traits: soy alto (I am tall). Estar is for states and locations: estoy cansado (I am tired), estoy en casa (I am at home). Mix them up and 'estoy aburrido' (I'm bored) becomes 'soy aburrido' (I'm a boring person).

cards.title: The big three you'll use daily
cards.body: Tener (to have), hacer (to do/make), ir (to go). Spanish says tengo hambre (I have hunger) instead of 'I am hungry', and voy a la tienda (I go to the store). These three unlock half of everyday speech.
Regular -ar verbs: drop the -ar, add -o, -as, -a, -amos, -an. Hablar → hablo, hablas, habla, hablamos, hablan. Learn the pattern once and hundreds of verbs follow it.

Hablar (to speak):
yo hablo — I speak
tú hablas — you speak
él/ella habla — he/she speaks

Same endings work for comprar (to buy), estudiar (to study), trabajar (to work). One pattern, endless verbs.

cards.q: You're hungry. What do you say?
cards.explain: Spanish uses tener for hunger: literally 'I have hunger.' Soy/estoy don't pair with hambre.

flashcards.front: Ser vs estar — what's the difference?
flashcards.back: Ser = permanent traits (soy alto). Estar = states and locations (estoy cansado).

flashcards.front: How do you say 'I am hungry'?
flashcards.back: Tengo hambre — Spanish uses 'to have' for hunger.

flashcards.front: What does 'ir' mean and give one form.

questions.q: 'Soy aburrido' vs 'estoy aburrido' — what's the difference?
choices: I am a boring person vs I am bored
questions.explain: Ser makes it a trait (boring person); estar makes it a state (bored right now). The verb changes the meaning.
The -amos ending marks 'we' for -ar verbs: hablamos.
Tener = to have, hacer = to do/make, ir = to go.

questions.q: Complete: Ella ___ en Madrid. (She is in Madrid.)
questions.explain: Locations always use estar. Es would describe what she is like, not where she is.
Voy is 'I go' from ir — one of the most-used words in the language.

cards.title: Getting what you need
cards.body: ¿Dónde está…? (where is…?), ¿Cuánto cuesta? (how much?), la cuenta, por favor (the bill, please). Three phrases handle shops, restaurants, and getting un-lost.

cards.title: Small talk that works
cards.body: ¿Cómo estás? (how are you?), me llamo… (my name is…), ¿hablas inglés? (do you speak English?). People appreciate the effort even when you switch to English after.
Tú is for friends and peers; usted is formal (strangers, elders, officials). When in doubt with someone older or in a formal setting, usted is the safe choice.

At a restaurant:
— ¿Una mesa para dos, por favor? (A table for two, please?)
— ¿Qué recomienda? (What do you recommend?)
— La cuenta, por favor. (The bill, please.)

Polite, complete, and you never touched English.

cards.q: Dinner's done. How do you ask for the bill?
cards.explain: La cuenta, por favor is the standard phrase. ¿Cuánto es asks the price of something specific.

flashcards.front: How do you ask for the bill?
How do you ask 'how much is it?'

questions.q: You're lost and need the station. You ask…
questions.explain: ¿Dónde está…? asks for locations. The others ask prices or make small talk.

questions.q: You want to know the price of a shirt. You say…
questions.explain: ¿Cuánto cuesta? = how much does it cost. La cuenta is the restaurant bill.

questions.q: Meeting someone your age at a party, you use…
questions.explain: Tú is for peers and friends. Usted is formal; vosotros is 'you all' (Spain).
Me llamo is literally 'I call myself' — the standard way to introduce yourself.

questions.q: A shopkeeper says '¿Algo más?' You hear…
questions.explain: ¿Algo más? = anything else? — the classic follow-up after your first request.
